nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the focus of the work mentioned in the paragraph regarding biocomposites?
nodes.answer: The work focuses on determining whether the novel biocomposite with antibacterial properties is a more environmentally friendly solution compared to conventional materials.
nodes.paragraph: In comparison to flax, hemp is coarser and stiffer and contains approx. 3% lignin while flax has only 2%. Like flax, hemp has a low elongation at break of up to 4%, a high strength of 40 80 cN/tex and moisture absorption of up to 30% [ 21]. Even though it is sometimes used as bio-based filler in construction and animal bedding the majority of the HH is disposed of by incineration or landfilling. When achieving a high yield per kg it has been used successfully in ethanol production. Hemp hurd exhibits antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli (E. coli) and has potential to be compounded with PLA, when using glycidyl methac - rylate (GMA) as compatibilizer [ 9]. Although LCAs of biocomposites have been performed, to the authors' knowledge, their antibacterial properties as a function have not been discussed in the literature in detail (see section Life Cycle Assessment ). Therefore, in this work we shall address the question of whether the novel biocomposite with its antibacterial properties is a more environmentally friendly solution compared to current con - ventional materials.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Eco-friendly construction materials|Eco-friendly composite materials_qna_001
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why are regenerated fibres like Lowell and Tents considered more eco-friendly than synthetic fibres?
nodes.answer: Regenerated fibres like Lowell and Tents are considered more eco-friendly than synthetic fibres due to their biodegradability and renewable source of raw material.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Eco-friendly construction materials|Eco-friendly composite materials_qna_002
nodes.label: Factual
nodes.question: Why is cotton often blended with synthetic fibres like polyester?
nodes.answer: Cotton is often blended with synthetic fibres like polyester to improve properties such as strength, durability, creasing properties, and ease of drying. This blending allows manufacturers to create fabrics that combine the best qualities of both natural and synthetic fibres for enhanced performance in clothing.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What applications are suggested for the magnetic composite materials developed in this study?
nodes.answer: The magnetic composite materials are suggested for use in electromagnetic shielding, which aims to reduce the electromagnetic field in specified areas.
nodes.paragraph: Frontal Polymerization (FP) is a technique that harnesses the chemi - cal energy stored within a resin to drive material synthesis. In this self-sustained process, an initial stimulus (e.g., thermal or photo) induces a localized reaction zone, the so-called polymerization front , which can propagate through the entire system without requiring further energy input. For instance, in Thermal Frontal Polymerization (TFP) the heat, i.e., the thermal trigger, is only applied to a small area of the sample and for a time interval that is short compared to the total cure time, see Fig. 1. The local increase in temperature triggers the polymerization of the reactants. Subsequently, the heat released by the curing process is transferred to the surrounding regions, promoting the creation of a hot reaction front that propagates to the unreacted regions of the reactants, thus converting them into polymer. TFP is the most widely studied mechanism, having the widest range of velocities, rates of conversion, and types of materials that can be used [ 3]. In general, FP requires highly exothermic polymerization processes, as well as efficient heat transport within the monomer solution for front propagation.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Eco-friendly construction materials|Eco-friendly composite materials_qna_004
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What unique properties make Fe3O4 nanoparticles an attractive filler for polymer composites?
nodes.answer: Fe3O4 nanoparticles exhibit unique properties such as superparamagnetism, low toxicity, high surface to volume ratio, easy synthesis, and biocompatibility, making them suitable for applications like electromagnetic shielding.
nodes.paragraph: Given the fact, that in TFP the polymerization is driven by a thermal front, the thermal conductivity of the reinforcing phase along with the reduced resin content is a crucial factor in understanding and controlling the reaction. The incorporation of highly conductive fillers alters the thermal transport characteristics during FP and it may allow heat from the polym - erization reaction to advance ahead of the front into the unreacted monomer, like experi - mentally and numerically shown by Goli et al. [ 5] for continuous conductive elements. Tran et al. [ 3] successfully evaluated the influence of various types of fillers (e.g., aluminium, glass microspheres, graphite, mica, ) on the FP behavior of a BADGE-based system. The authors found that the reduction in monomer fraction led to a reduction in heat generation, while the fillers also absorbed parts of heat, resulting in a declined frontal velocity and tem - perature with increasing filler content. Instabilities in FP due to the addition of fillers, i.e., an increased energy dissipation and reduced availability of exothermic energy as the volume fraction of the resin decreases with increasing filler content, were also reported by Suslick et at [ 4].

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Eco-friendly construction materials|Eco-friendly composite materials_qna_005
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What unique properties make Fe3O4 nanoparticles attractive for use in polymer composites?
nodes.answer: Fe3O4 nanoparticles are attractive due to their superparamagnetism, low toxicity, high surface to volume ratio, easy synthesis, and biocompatibility, making them suitable for applications such as electromagnetic shielding.
nodes.paragraph: Further efforts to study the effects of added fillers (glass, steel, carbon) include the publications of Kumar et al. [ 6] who presented analytical expressions for the velocity of the self-propagating reaction front in the FP of thermoset polymers and composites, Vyas et al. [10] who presented a numerical study of the manufacturing of unidirectional glass-fiber- reinforced composites via FP, Wang et al. [ 9] who investigated the effect of fiber volume fraction on the average front velocity and the maximum temperature in the FP process, and Centellas et al. [ 10] who investigated the effect of multiple polymerization fronts on the composite cure time, quality, and mechanical performance. However, the detailed investi - gation of the influence of different filling degrees (in particular with respect to composites with high filling degrees on inorganic particles) using mathematical modeling & numerical simulation routines, is still in its infancy. With respect to curing kinetics, publications are either based on the determination of cur - ing kinetics of the unfilled resin, ignoring the influence of the filler content on curing kinet - ics, e.g., by Wang et al.
